analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license with training and background checks to buy a gun.
analysis.headline: The licensing bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it unlawful to buy or receive a firearm without a federal license from the Department of Justice. To get one, a person would have to pass a firearms safety class with a written test and live firing test, submit fingerprints, and clear a background investigation. Licenses would cover a single gun purchase within 30 days, private sales would have to go through a licensed dealer for background checks, and all gun transactions would have to be reported to the Justice Department within three business days.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would have been people exposed to gun violence, since the bill aimed to keep firearms away from people judged a danger to themselves or others and to close the private-sale loophole in background checks. State and local officials could flag dangerous applicants directly to the Justice Department.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every buyer to obtain a federal license after passing safety training and a background investigation, and lets the Attorney General deny licenses to people deemed a significant danger of bodily injury, with court review of denials [S3].
Requires private gun sales to go through a licensed dealer for a background check, closing the loophole that lets unlicensed sellers transfer guns without one [S3].

Requires sellers to report every gun transaction to the Justice Department within three business days, with buyer and gun details, and allows states with substantially similar licensing to substitute their own system [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Lawful gun buyers would bear the cost of training, testing, fees, and waiting for a license for each gun, and a license would cover just one firearm used within 30 days. Gun manufacturers and dealers would face a smaller market, and the Justice Department would carry the cost of running a national licensing, investigation, and transaction-reporting system.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun buyers, the firearms industry, DOJ

drawbacks.text: Each license covers a single firearm and must be used within 30 days, so a buyer wanting more than one gun would repeat the full process each time, adding cost and delay for lawful owners [S3].

Applicants must pass hands-on firing and accuracy testing and a written test on firearms law, which would impose a real barrier for people who want a gun for self-defense and cannot easily reach a training site, especially in rural areas, though the bill requires licensing offices in both urban and rural areas [S3].

The Attorney General could deny or revoke a license based on a broad list of factors, including drug or alcohol abuse history and recent gun purchases, which critics would call an unusually wide grant of discretion over a constitutional right, though denials and revocations would be reviewable in federal court [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is an ambitious universal licensing system that would meaningfully restrict dangerous people's access to guns, at a genuine cost in time, money, and paperwork for millions of lawful buyers. Whether that tradeoff is worth it is a legitimate disagreement; what is not disputed is that the bill never got far enough for anyone to vote on it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then sent to its crime subcommittee, and sat there with no hearings, no committee vote, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Kim of New Jersey introduced the bill on July 27, 2022, joined by Rep. Carolyn Maloney of New York as its only cosponsor [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, and on November 1, 2022, referred it again to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security [S5].
No further action was recorded before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died without a vote in either chamber [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The firearms industry and gun owners who opposed federal licensing are better off, since no license requirement was ever enacted; people hoping for federal gun licensing gained nothing, and the status quo of no federal license to buy a gun continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firearms industry and opposing gun owners

for.name: Rep. Andy Kim
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on July 27, 2022

against.name: Rep. Jerry Nadler
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to committee action; after the November 1 referral to the crime subcommittee, no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled [S5]

against.name: Gun rights organizations such as the National Rifle Association
against.role: Opposition movement against federal gun licensing
against.what_they_did: Long-standing opposition to federal licensing and universal background checks shaped the climate in which no committee moved the bill

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had only Democratic sponsorship (one sponsor and one cosponsor) and no Republican support, but the lack of any recorded action keeps the partisan split untested.

industries.note: A license covering a single gun purchase, mandatory dealer-run checks on private sales, and three-day transaction reporting would shrink legal sales volumes and add compliance costs. The industry's interest in continuing unrestricted sales runs against the bill's public-safety goal.
The bill would require a written test plus hands-on firing test for every applicant, creating a national customer base for safety training providers.
